edition: Issue 039: The party that wouldn't take the call now wants a relationship, the Kiwis and Kangaroos book their fourth World Cup final, and Auckland's beaches take a rain check after the storm did the plumbing's job
tagline: Your 3-minute Monday reset: Qiulae Wong's phone logs two calls (Hipkins, Swarbrick), zero from Luxon - who now says he 'does want to talk to her' - while the country waits on special votes and runs on caretaker autopilot; the Kiwis beat Tonga 34-10 and book a Brisbane World Cup final with the Kangaroos, the fourth time the codes' two biggest families have met in the decider; and about a dozen Waitematā Harbour beaches go on the no-swim list after election-weekend storms flushed the network's pipes into the harbour.

stories.headline: The most sought-after number in Wellington belongs to Qiulae Wong: two calls so far, neither from Luxon, who now says he 'does want to talk to her'
stories.summary: Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong has taken calls from Labour's Chris Hipkins and the Greens' Chlöe Swarbrick but not yet from Christopher Luxon, who told Newstalk ZB he intends to call and 'wants a relationship'; her caucus meets this week with two anonymous negotiators in the room, the country runs under the caretaker convention, and official results land 27 November.

body.text: While roughly 600,000 special votes sit uncounted, New Zealand has begun the most unpredictable negotiating season MMP has produced - and the diary that matters now belongs to a party that reached Parliament from the cold for the very first time. Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong took calls over the weekend from Labour's Chris Hipkins and the Greens' Chlöe Swarbrick; as of Monday morning, National leader Christopher Luxon's name was not among them, though he said on Monday he intends to fix that: 'I do want to have a relationship and I do want to talk to her' - a soft landing for a campaign spent ruling her party out. Wong says she will talk to the largest party first, which on the preliminary numbers is National, but that 'just because we speak to the largest party first doesn't guarantee anything'. Her caucus meets this week ahead of new-MP school at Parliament on Tuesday; the party constitution hands its board a sign-off role over any agreement, and two members of its negotiating team remain anonymous - public servants, Wong says, whose privacy must be respected. All of it happens under the caretaker convention: Luxon's ministers stay in office and significant decisions get deferred while five electorates stay uncomfortably close (Wairarapa by 139 votes) and official results land on 27 November.

'I do want to talk to her' is the most romantic sentence in New Zealand politics this week - the equivalent of nine months of 'we're not a fit', followed by a Monday-morning realisation that the only caterer in town is lovely, available, and keeping a diary. Wong's weekend phone log: two calls, both from the left, both cheerful, coffee to come. National's team is presumably still checking whether the parliamentary handsets are wireless. Then there is the transparency detail: Opportunity's stationery says 'transparency at the heart of politics', and its negotiating team contains two people so secret they are unnamed public servants - which is how you know every workplace in the country is suddenly fascinated. The board's sign-off is this week's most scrutinised swing factor, with Shane Jones diagnosing 'a strange quirkiness' in Opportunity's constitution, which is how you can tell MMP has achieved peak content. New-MP school starts Tuesday: bring a pen, and for the love of democracy, a phone that holds a charge.

NZ Herald election live updates (9 Nov 2026): Wong told Mike Hosking Breakfast and TV1's Breakfast she spoke to Hipkins and Swarbrick over the weekend - 'but not National leader Christopher Luxon yet' - and did not rule out working with National; Luxon said on Monday he 'does want to have a relationship and [does] want to talk to her', acknowledged coalition negotiations with two partners may be 'more difficult this time around', and said 'If the choice is a hung Parliament, New Zealanders are not going to thank you (for) going back to the polls'. NZ Herald (Ethan Manera, 9 Nov, premium): two members of Opportunity's negotiating team are anonymous public servants; the party campaigned on putting 'transparency at the heart of politics'. RNZ (Lauren Crimp, 8 Nov): Opportunity is the first party to enter Parliament from outside MMP; Wong's options are coalition, confidence and supply, or cross benches; bottom lines include regulating lobbying; new-MP school begins Tuesday 10 November. Caretaker convention (The Conversation via RNZ, 8 Nov): Luxon and ministers remain in office; significant or controversial decisions deferred or made in consultation; Wairarapa provisionally National's Mike Butterick by 139 votes; special votes tend left; official results 27 November. Helen Clark (Herald/AAP, 9 Nov) called for a full review of the electoral system. ACT's David Seymour and NZ First's Shane Jones said they have not yet spoken to Luxon since election night (Herald live, 9 Nov).

stories.headline: Kiwis vs Kangaroos, the reunion special: Brisbane books a fourth World Cup final between the game's two biggest families
stories.summary: The Kiwis beat Tonga 34-10 in Newcastle to reach their first Rugby League World Cup final since 2013, where they meet the Kangaroos - 44-12 winners over Samoa with a Reece Walsh hat-trick - at Suncorp Stadium next Sunday, in a repeat of the 2000, 2008 and 2013 deciders; the Kiwi Ferns are in the women's final too.

body.text: The Rugby League World Cup final on Sunday 15 November at Suncorp Stadium in Brisbane will feature exactly the two teams you suspect it will feature, because it always features these two teams. The Kiwis earned their ticket in Newcastle on Saturday, beating Tonga 34-10 at McDonald Jones Stadium to reach a first World Cup final since 2013, with Kalyn Ponga back in the side. Australia joined them on Sunday night, brushing aside Samoa 44-12 in their semi-final at Allianz Stadium in Sydney - a Reece Walsh hat-trick anchoring the win in front of a crowd pushing past 41,000 - to set up a decider that is both a rematch of the Round 1 pool game in Sydney on 15 October and a repeat of the 2000, 2008 and 2013 finals, in which the Kiwis' last title, in 2008, came at Suncorp itself with a Benji Marshall-inspired upset. The women's final that same weekend is also Australia v New Zealand: the Kiwi Ferns swept into the decider to replay the 2022 double-header. Whoever wins, one of the two flags gets a very long weekend.

Australia v New Zealand in a rugby league World Cup final is less a fixture than a family reunion: they have now done this in 2000, 2008, 2013 and 2026, and every host venue knows the seating plan by heart - Brisbane's Suncorp is basically a bach with a big mortgage. The Kangaroos arrived via a 44-12 semi-final where Reece Walsh scored a hat-trick with the air of a tour guide showing off three brand-new car parks; Samoa rallied for a second-half laugh and still went home with the brochure, which is a shame, because nobody at the reunion is more fun than Samoa. The Kiwis, who politely showed Tonga the door 34-10, have not lifted this particular trophy since 2008, the year Benji Marshall's team produced the kind of upset grandparents still mention at every barbecue - conveniently at Suncorp, which is why the venue should technically be grandfathered into our folklore. Add the women's decider, also Australia v New Zealand, and Brisbane gets a double-feature platter fit for both national budgets. One request for the organisers: leave the trophy room unlocked, because if history repeats itself exactly, we are due for the good ending this time.

RNZ (8 Nov 2026, 'Rugby League World Cup: Kiwis kick Tonga out on way to final'): New Zealand beat Tonga 34-10 in the semi-final at McDonald Jones Stadium, Newcastle (played Saturday 7 November NZT), ending Tonga's run and reaching a first World Cup final since 2013; Kalyn Ponga returned for the semis (RNZ team naming). NZ Herald (Ben Francis, 8 Nov): Australia beat Samoa 44-12 at Allianz Stadium, Sydney; Reece Walsh scored three tries; Samoa led 3-0 on a Stephen Crichton penalty; Crichton and Izack Tago scored second-half tries for Samoa. NRL.com match report (8 Nov): 41,259 fans at Allianz Stadium; the final is at Suncorp Stadium, Brisbane, next Sunday (15 November), a rematch of the Round 1 Pool A game in Sydney (15 Oct) and 'a repeat of the 2013, 2008 and 2000 World Cup Finals'; the 2008 final produced 'one of the biggest upsets in World Cup history when the Benji Marshall-inspired Kiwis got home 34-20'; Australia and New Zealand will also meet in the women's final, 'just as it was in 2022 in the UK'.

stories.headline: Election weekend's real runoff: the storm flushed Auckland's pipes, and about a dozen Waitematā Harbour beaches are off the swim list
stories.summary: After severe thunderstorms swept the North Island - nearly 1,850 lightning strikes from midnight Friday, a roof down in Wairau Valley, the Auckland-Phoenix derby delayed - untreated wastewater overflowed into the Waitematā Harbour, and Safeswim has beaches from Okahu Bay to Herne Bay under no-swim notices, with more severe thunderstorm warnings issued for Monday.

body.text: The severe thunderstorms that swept the North Island over the weekend have blown over, but they left their homework in Auckland's water. About a dozen beaches on the Waitematā Harbour are now off-limits after the stormwater swamped the network and untreated wastewater overflowed near popular bathing spots: Safeswim has deemed the Tāmaki Drive beaches from Okahu Bay to St Heliers unsafe to enter, along with Orakei Basin, Te Tinana, Herne Bay and Home Bay, with a further four North Shore beaches carrying the same warning and digital signs at Browns Bay, Takapuna, St Mary's Bay and Herne Bay. The storm that did the damage was spectacular while it lasted: Fire and Emergency logged nearly 1,845 lightning strikes from midnight Friday, downpours reached 33.5mm an hour in the Bay of Plenty, a roof collapsed at a Wairau Valley house, a Totara Vale house flooded, a Grey Lynn billboard came down across a footpath and cycle lane, and lightning delayed the kick-off of the Auckland FC-Wellington Phoenix derby. Fire and Emergency reported no known threats to life. And the weather is not done negotiating: Stuff reports new severe thunderstorm warnings for Auckland and Waikato on Monday, with flash flooding and possible 40mm downpours.

There is a special poetry to an election weekend in which the city's biggest runoff took place not in a cabinet room but in the Waitematā: the rain did its civic duty, the pipes folded like a minister under questioning, and a dozen beaches now fly the unofficial flag of 'please swim literally anywhere else'. Safeswim has just opened summer by banning the harbour's most popular swim spots - every first dip of the season, postponed by the plumbing equivalent of a hung parliament. Before you judge the water, be kind: it has been asked to absorb both the city's stormwater and its confidence votes, and it has had enough of both. The good news: Mission Bay will be back, the sun does not require council consent, and the only thing the storm failed to interrupt was the special votes, which are, as far as we can tell, waterproof. Monday has scheduled more thunder for Auckland and Waikato, so keep the floaties dry and the weather app closer than the beach towel. And when in doubt, trust the ducks - they are working from home this week.

NZ Herald (Tom Eley, 8 Nov 2026, 6:26pm): about a dozen Waitematā Harbour beaches contaminated with untreated wastewater after weekend storms overflowed near popular bathing spots; eight inner-city bays 'deemed unfit to enter' plus four on the North Shore; Safeswim warnings covered the Tāmaki Drive beaches from Okahu Bay to St Heliers, Orakei Basin, Te Tinana, Herne Bay and Home Bay; digital signs displayed advice at Browns Bay, Takapuna, St Mary's Bay and Herne Bay; swimmers advised to check Safeswim before entering. RNZ (7 Nov 2026, 6:45pm): MetService lifted all severe thunderstorm watches and warnings after the storms passed; nearly 1,845 lightning strikes recorded from midnight Friday; downpours to 33.5mm/h in the Bay of Plenty; Fire and Emergency reported 'no known threats to life'; roof collapse at a Wairau Valley house; flooding in a Totara Vale house; a billboard came down in Grey Lynn overnight Friday; lightning delayed the Auckland FC v Wellington Phoenix derby kick-off; a Cotton On store roof in Blenheim collapsed 'because of rain build up' with no injuries, and the shop reopened. Stuff (9 Nov 2026): new severe thunderstorm warnings issued for Auckland and Waikato, with the potential for flash flooding and 40mm downpours.

affiliate_cta.headline: Beaches off-limits and a government on hold? Before you buy the escape, here's the calm look-around.
affiliate_cta.body: Today's edition is a waiting room: Auckland beaches on no-swim notices, coalition maths on a three-week count, and a World Cup final still a week away. If all this waiting has you about to spend - a last-minute summer trip, new gear for big-match Sunday, or anything with a waterproof rating - take a calm look around before you commit. No pitch, no pressure, just the specs.
